triadic-tetradic-color-generator.quickAnswer: These schemes place hues at equal steps around the wheel. From #FF5733 (hue 11): triadic adds 120 and 240 -> #33FF58 and #5833FF; square adds 90, 180, 270 for four colors; tetradic (rectangular) adds 60, 180, 240. Equal spacing is why they feel balanced even when the colors are bold.
keyFacts: Triadic = 3 hues at 0, 120, 240 degrees: the classic vibrant-but-balanced trio.
Square = 4 hues at 0, 90, 180, 270: even energy in every direction.
Tetradic (rectangular) = 0, 60, 180, 240: two close pairs, rich and complex.
Equal spacing is what makes geometric schemes feel intentional.
With 3-4 strong hues, always crown one as dominant (60%+) or the design fights itself.
howTo: Enter your base color with the picker or a HEX code like #FF5733.
The scheme appears instantly with hue labels and HEX codes.
Tap any swatch to copy its HEX.
Pick one color as dominant and use the rest as accents.
triadic-tetradic-color-generator.formula:
Scheme color = HSL((base hue + offset) mod 360, S, L).
Triadic offsets: 0, 120, 240. Square offsets: 0, 90, 180, 270. Tetradic offsets: 0, 60, 180, 240.
Example: #FF5733 -> HSL(11, 100%, 60%), triadic:
+120 -> HSL(131, 100%, 60%) = RGB(51, 255, 88) = #33FF58.
+240 -> HSL(251, 100%, 60%) = RGB(88, 51, 255) = #5833FF.

4. Final trio: orange-red #FF5733, green #33FF58, violet #5833FF - three hues an equal 120 degrees apart.
benefits: Three geometric schemes from one color in a single tap.

limitations: Bold by construction - these schemes are rarely subtle.

faqs.q: What is the difference between tetradic and square?
faqs.a: Both have four colors. Square spaces them evenly at 90 degrees (0, 90, 180, 270). Tetradic uses a rectangle: 0, 60, 180, 240 - two close pairs opposite each other, which feels richer but needs more careful balancing.

faqs.q: Which scheme is best for beginners?
faqs.a: Triadic. Three colors is manageable, and the 120-degree spacing is forgiving - it is the scheme behind countless logos and illustrations.

faqs.q: How do I stop four colors from clashing?
faqs.a: Give one color 60-70% of the space, a second 20-30%, and use the remaining two as small accents. Hierarchy tames even the boldest scheme.

faqs.q: Can I use these for data charts?
faqs.a: Triadic works well for 3-series charts. For more series, take the scheme hues and vary lightness to create distinguishable-but-related colors.

faqs.q: Why do the schemes keep my saturation and lightness?
faqs.a: Fixed saturation and lightness keep every color in the same intensity family, so the geometry of the hues is what you see - not random brightness jumps.

faqs.q: Do these work in dark mode?
faqs.a: The hue relationships hold in any mode. For dark mode, lower the lightness of the dominant color's usage as background and keep one hue bright for accents.
